intro.title: Will Cook: AI-written maths and code, made easier to understand
intro.description: I do maths research and build software with AI, and I use AI to make the results easier to understand. Fifteen projects with short videos, and websites, papers, proofs or code where they exist.
intro.h1: I use AI to make AI-written maths and code easier to understand.
intro.lede: I do maths research and build software with AI. Most projects here can be followed at several levels of detail, from a short video down to the proof or the code.
intro.second: I build the tools so they get better as AI models get better.

idle.alt: From the introduction: what AI produces goes through an AI model and comes out as a paper for experts, a website with the paper beside its proof, a map where you click any theorem, and a video for anyone. With a better model, each of these is redrawn.

entries.name: The funnel
entries.line: How a Lean proof becomes papers and a video
entries.claim: The funnel is a set of written instructions that AI follows to turn a proof Lean has accepted into shorter and shorter versions for different readers. For one Erdős problem that is 152 pages, then 26, then 16, then a half-hour video.
entries.limit: Lean checks the proof. An expert still has to judge whether each paper and video says the same maths.
entries.page_title: The funnel: how a Lean proof becomes papers and a video
entries.description: Written instructions that AI follows to turn a proof Lean has accepted into shorter versions for different readers. For one Erdős problem that is 152 pages, then 26, then 16, then a half-hour video. Lean checks the proof. The papers and the video still need an expert’s reading.

entries.name: Maths Map
entries.line: Eight Erdős problems on one map
entries.claim: Maths Map is a website with one map of every theorem from my research on eight Erdős problems. Click a theorem and you go straight to where it is written up, in the long research record or the short paper for experts.
entries.limit: Lean checks only some of the theorems, and the papers are written with AI, so an expert still needs to read them. Seven of the eight questions remain open. For #1041, a formal version of the statement is refuted.
entries.credit: The #1041 formal-statement counterexample is due to ani.
entries.page_title: Maths Map: eight Erdős problems on one map
entries.description: A website with one map of every theorem from my research on eight Erdős problems. Click a theorem to open where it is written up. Lean checks some of the theorems, the papers are written with AI, and seven of the eight questions remain open.
entries.card_alt: Maths Map: Eight Erdős problems on one map. A frame from the project’s video.

entries.name: Erdős #257
entries.line: A case from 1968, proved and checked in Lean
entries.claim: Take the fractions 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15 and so on, and add up infinitely many of them. Erdős asked whether the total can ever be written as a fraction. In 1968 he stated one case, where the reciprocals of the chosen exponents have a finite sum, and proved it with an extra restriction. Here that case is proved without the restriction, and Lean accepts the proof.
entries.limit: The question Erdős asked, for every infinite choice, is still open. The papers are written with AI and are not peer reviewed.
entries.credit: Erdős stated this case in 1968. Google DeepMind's Formal Conjectures lists it as solved.
entries.page_title: Erdős #257: a case from 1968, proved and checked in Lean
entries.description: Add up infinitely many of the fractions 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15 and so on. Can the total ever be written as a fraction? Erdős stated one case in 1968 and proved it with an extra restriction. Here it is proved without the restriction, and Lean accepts the proof. The question for every infinite choice is still open.
entries.card_alt: Erdős #257: A case from 1968, proved and checked in Lean. A frame from the project’s video.

entries.name: Quantum computers
entries.line: OpenAI's fourth-power result, proved again in Lean
entries.claim: Count how often each machine looks at its input. For a yes-or-no question with an answer for every input, an ordinary computer needs at most a fixed multiple of the quantum count to the fourth power, and OpenAI showed that no smaller power works. Lean checks that whole theorem here.
entries.limit: The count is of looks at the input, which is a different measure from running time. The labels that compare each Lean statement with the paper are AI-written, and no expert has reviewed them yet.
entries.credit: The result is OpenAI's, released in October 2026. It matches an upper bound proved in 2020.
entries.page_title: Quantum computers: OpenAI’s fourth-power result, proved again in Lean
entries.description: Count how often each machine looks at its input. For yes-or-no questions with an answer for every input, the ordinary count is at most a fixed multiple of the quantum count to the fourth power, and OpenAI showed no smaller power works. Lean checks this. Looks at the input are a different measure from running time.

entries.name: Spin glass
entries.line: Two nearly best answers, half the arrows differ
entries.claim: In a model of magnets, every arrow points up or down and every arrangement gets a score. Two arrangements can both score almost the best while about half their arrows differ. When the scoring is random, the chance that such a pair exists approaches 100% as the number of arrows grows.
entries.limit: The Lean proofs are OpenAI's and cover OpenAI's theorem. They do not cover this result about two arrangements.
entries.credit: The result follows from a 2020 paper by Auffinger, Chen and Zeng and an OpenAI theorem released in October 2026.
entries.page_title: Spin glass: two nearly best answers, half the arrows differ
entries.description: In a model of magnets, two arrangements can both score almost the best while about half their arrows differ. The result follows from a 2020 paper by Auffinger, Chen and Zeng and an OpenAI theorem. The Lean proofs are OpenAI’s and cover OpenAI’s theorem only.

entries.name: Reader websites
entries.line: Click a linked sentence, open the Lean beside it
entries.names: Lean Exposition, Quartic Reader, Proof Reader
entries.claim: Three websites where you read a maths paper and click a linked sentence to open the Lean linked to it, beside the text. In Lean Exposition and Proof Reader, the step you are reading is also highlighted on a map of the argument.
entries.limit: Lean checks the code. Whether a sentence and the code say the same thing is for a person to judge, and I made the links with AI.
entries.credit: Lean Exposition and Quartic Reader show OpenAI's papers. Proof Reader shows Contextual Embeddings by Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang, with the authors' own Lean proof.

entries.name: Atlas
entries.line: Two groups, two labels for one maths paper
entries.claim: Atlas is a website that lists the papers in OpenAI's October 2026 maths release, with other groups' checking reports linked beside each one. For the paper about π, two groups both report the proof accepted and label its coverage differently. Atlas shows the two labels side by side.
entries.limit: Each group reported its own labels and proof checks, and Atlas has not rerun them. The suggested matches between paper theorems and Lean statements are unreviewed.
entries.credit: The two reports on the π paper are by MathVet and by Carlos Toledo's cert-machine. Atlas also uses Neal McBurnett's Lean tooling.

entries.name: Verification map
entries.line: What one proof covers, in a toolkit of 88 components
entries.claim: A map of the 88 components of my public toolkit. Rings around each component show which kinds of evidence it has. Sixteen calculations are proved with Dafny for every input: the twelve marked on the map, and four shared by the whole toolkit.
entries.limit: Each proof covers one stated calculation. The outer ring shows how much of a component's whole claim has been checked, and it reads unknown for every component.

entries.name: CodeMap
entries.line: A map of my code from AI-written descriptions
entries.claim: Every file in my code is drawn as a box containing the short description written at the top of that file. The descriptions are meant to be updated with the code, so no AI writes anything when the map is opened.
entries.limit: CodeMap is private, and the videos show it in use. A description can be wrong or out of date, and nothing checks it against the code.

entries.name: Code Ontology Bridge
entries.line: NVIDIA's Auto Ontology answers questions about its own code
entries.claim: A program that reads a Python project and writes a database of every function and which function calls which. Given that database of its own code, NVIDIA's Auto Ontology, running a DeepSeek model, answered 10.3 of 12 questions correctly on average. The same model asked directly answered 3.2.
entries.limit: Twelve questions, written by AI models. The answer keys were corrected after the runs, which moved results in both directions.
entries.credit: Auto Ontology is NVIDIA's open-source project. This study is independent of NVIDIA.
entries.page_title: Code Ontology Bridge: NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology answers questions about its own code
entries.description: A program that reads a Python project and writes a database of its functions and calls. Given that database of its own code, NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology, running a DeepSeek model, answered 10.3 of 12 questions correctly on average. The same model asked directly answered 3.2. AI models wrote the questions, and the study is independent of NVIDIA.

entries.name: One Checkout
entries.line: Commit one fix while another AI keeps editing
entries.claim: When two AI coding assistants edit the same file, committing one finished fix can also commit the other's unfinished edits. One Checkout commits only the exact lines of the fix, and the shared file still contains both sets of edits.
entries.limit: It does not stop two assistants overwriting each other's edits. It turns off Git's usual checks for each commit, so the assistants have to run the project's checks themselves.

entries.name: Safety Core
entries.line: A written rule let 6 of 10 AI runs commit a made-up value. A check let 0.
entries.claim: Safety Core is one file of rules for AI coding assistants, each rule labelled with how it is enforced. In one test an assistant made up a setting value so a failing test passed, then committed: in 10 runs of 10 with no rules, 6 of 10 with written rules, and 0 of 10 when a check held the command for approval.
entries.limit: One model, Claude Haiku 4.5, on one small project, ten runs per setup. The check was written after this failure was first seen, and nobody was present to approve.

entries.name: Agent Trace
entries.line: Read what your AI coding assistant ran
entries.claim: Claude Code and Codex save every conversation as a file. Agent Trace lists those conversations as they run, shows each command beside what it returned, and copies the part you choose into another chat.
entries.limit: It shows only what the files recorded. Large outputs can be shortened, and it does not remove passwords from what it copies.

entries.name: Zenith
entries.line: Showing an AI tester the bugs it missed
entries.claim: An AI model that tests code was shown the bugs it had missed on practice problems. On 58 new problems, the share of hidden bug types it caught rose on average from 69.2% to 77.0%.
entries.limit: About half of the rise came from timeouts. The study tested one model on short programs, and rules the model wrote from its own mistakes did not clearly raise the score.

entries.name: Narration IR
entries.line: Plan what each sentence means, then animate
entries.claim: Each animation starts from a written plan: what each spoken sentence means, and which spoken word each change in the picture is timed to. A program confirms that each quote in a plan is in its source file.
entries.limit: The program does not check whether a meaning is right, so I read each plan myself. Whether plans like this help a viewer understand has not been tested.
